NBA Expected Field-Goal Percentage — a SEMMA Project¶

Author: Meron Tesfandrias · Course: CMPE 255 · Repo: MeronDT/CMPE-255-Data-Mining-process · App: <deployed URL>

Data: NBA shot-chart detail (stats.nba.com), compiled by shufinskiy/nba_data (Apache-2.0; also on Kaggle). Every regular-season field-goal attempt with court coordinates, shot type, game clock and outcome. Population: five seasons, 2019-20 → 2023-24 (1,031,740 shots). Out-of-time check: 2024-25 (219,527 shots).

SEMMA (SAS Institute) organises the technical core of data mining into five steps. Each step below maps to the SAS Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it, so the same flow can be rebuilt in SAS (see the appendix).

Step Purpose Enterprise Miner nodes used here
Sample draw a representative, manageable sample; partition it Input Data · Sample · Data Partition
Explore understand distributions, relationships, anomalies StatExplore · MultiPlot / Graph Explore · Variable Selection · Cluster
Modify create, select, transform variables Drop · Transform Variables · Replacement · Interactive Binning · Impute
Model fit competing predictive models Regression · Decision Tree · Neural Network · Gradient Boosting · Ensemble
Assess compare models, check reliability, score new data Model Comparison · Cutoff · Score · Segment Profile

Headline result: a gradient-boosting model that estimates the make probability of any shot from where and how it is taken. It beats both the zone-average baseline and a stronger zone × shot-family baseline on every partition and on the unseen 2024-25 season (log loss 0.637 vs 0.647 and 0.658). It is calibrated to within 1.5 percentage points in every decile and within 2.1 points for every shot zone and shot family (except backcourt heaves). Most of the gain over location alone comes from the scorer's shot-type label (A.1). Comparing players' actual FG% with the xFG% of their shots separates shot making from shot selection. The gap persists from season to season (r = 0.70, 95 % CI 0.60–0.78, 131 players), though less than raw FG% does (0.86). So it is best read as shot-making plus context the model cannot see, not as pure skill.

How to run: Runtime → Run all (≈ 4–6 min on free Colab). Every figure, table, the model and the app are written to artifacts/.

Project context (pre-SEMMA)¶

SEMMA assumes the problem is already defined — unlike CRISP-DM it has no Business Understanding phase — so the problem is stated briefly here, to justify later choices.

  • Question: given where and how a shot is taken (location, shot type, game clock), what is the probability it goes in? This is expected field-goal percentage (xFG%) — a measure of shot quality, independent of who shoots.
  • Why it matters: raw FG% mixes two things: which shots a player takes and how well he makes them. A center who only dunks has a high FG% without being a great shooter. Comparing actual FG% with the xFG% of the same shots separates shot selection from shot making — the same idea as moving from box-score stats to advanced metrics when judging MVP candidates.
  • Target: SHOT_MADE_FLAG (1 = made). Unit: one field-goal attempt.
  • Success criteria: the champion model must
    1. beat a zone-average baseline (league FG% for the shot's official court zone) in validation log loss. A stronger zone × shot-family baseline is also reported, so the gain is not just "the model knows the shot type";
    2. be calibrated (predicted ≈ actual within each probability band, and within each shot zone and shot family);
    3. hold its performance on the unseen 2024-25 season.

SAMPLE_SIZE  = 200_000          # shots drawn from the population (justified by the learning curve in S.3)

def draw_court(ax, color="#555", lw=1.2):
    """NBA half court in shot-chart units (tenths of feet, hoop at 0,0)."""
    from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Rectangle, Arc
    for p in [Circle((0, 0), 7.5, fill=False), Rectangle((-30, -7.5), 60, 0), Rectangle((-80, -47.5), 160, 190, fill=False),
              Arc((0, 142.5), 120, 120, theta1=0, theta2=180), Arc((0, 0), 80, 80, theta1=0, theta2=180),
              Rectangle((-220, -47.5), 0, 140), Rectangle((220, -47.5), 0, 140), Arc((0, 0), 475, 475, theta1=22, theta2=158),
              Rectangle((-250, -47.5), 500, 470, fill=False)]:
        p.set_edgecolor(color); p.set_linewidth(lw); ax.add_patch(p)
    ax.set_xlim(-250, 250); ax.set_ylim(-47.5, 422.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

S — Sample¶

Goal: extract a portion of the data that is large enough to contain the significant information, yet small enough to process quickly — and partition it for honest model assessment.

S.1 Input Data¶

In [3]:
def load_season(season):
    path = DATA / f"shotdetail_{season}.csv"
    if not path.exists():                                  # download once, then reuse
        archive = DATA / f"shotdetail_{season}.tar.xz"
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL_TEMPLATE.format(season=season), archive)
        with tarfile.open(archive, "r:xz") as t:
            t.extractall(DATA)
        archive.unlink()
    d = pd.read_csv(path, dtype={c: "category" for c in ["GRID_TYPE", "PLAYER_NAME", "TEAM_NAME", "EVENT_TYPE", "ACTION_TYPE",
                                                         "SHOT_TYPE", "SHOT_ZONE_BASIC", "SHOT_ZONE_AREA", "SHOT_ZONE_RANGE", "HTM", "VTM"]})
    d.insert(0, "SEASON", f"{season}-{str(season + 1)[-2:]}")
    return d

t0 = time.time()
population = pd.concat([load_season(s) for s in POPULATION_SEASONS], ignore_index=True)
for c in population.select_dtypes("object").columns:
    population[c] = population[c].astype("category")
print(f"Population: {len(population):,} shots x {population.shape[1]} columns, {population['GAME_ID'].nunique():,} games "
      f"({time.time() - t0:.0f}s, {population.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.0f} MB)")
display(population.groupby("SEASON", observed=True).agg(shots=(TARGET, "size"), games=("GAME_ID", "nunique"), fg_pct=(TARGET, "mean")).round(3))
population.head(3)

The 2019-20 (COVID suspension and bubble) and 2020-21 (72-game) seasons have fewer games, but shooting barely differs between seasons (FG% 46.0–47.5 %), so pooling all five seasons is reasonable. Rising FG% in 2022-23 and 2023-24 is worth remembering for the out-of-time test.

S.2 Sample¶

In [4]:
# Proportional stratified sample: preserves each season's share and its make/miss mix
frac = SAMPLE_SIZE / len(population)
sampled = population.groupby(["SEASON", TARGET], observed=True, group_keys=False).sample(frac=frac, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
remainder = population.drop(sampled.index)          # the shots NOT drawn - an independent comparison group
sample = sampled.reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Sample: {len(sample):,} shots ({len(sample) / len(population):.1%}); per-stratum rounding gives {SAMPLE_SIZE - len(sample)} fewer than configured")

# Representativeness. FG% and season shares match BY DESIGN (they are the strata), so they are not evidence.
# The real test compares the sample with the unsampled remainder on variables that were NOT stratified on.
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp, chi2_contingency
def chi2_p(col, top=20):
    keep = remainder[col].value_counts().index[:top]
    pool = lambda s: s.astype(str).where(s.isin(keep), "other").value_counts()
    return chi2_contingency(pd.concat([pool(sample[col]), pool(remainder[col])], axis=1).fillna(0).T)[1]
check = pd.DataFrame([
    {"variable": "FG% (stratum - matches by design)", "sample": sample[TARGET].mean(), "remainder": remainder[TARGET].mean(), "test": "-", "p_value": np.nan},
    {"variable": "shot distance (mean ft)", "sample": sample["SHOT_DISTANCE"].mean(), "remainder": remainder["SHOT_DISTANCE"].mean(),
     "test": "KS", "p_value": ks_2samp(sample["SHOT_DISTANCE"], remainder["SHOT_DISTANCE"]).pvalue},
    {"variable": "LOC_X (mean)", "sample": sample["LOC_X"].mean(), "remainder": remainder["LOC_X"].mean(),
     "test": "KS", "p_value": ks_2samp(sample["LOC_X"], remainder["LOC_X"]).pvalue},
    {"variable": "3PT share", "sample": (sample["SHOT_TYPE"] == "3PT Field Goal").mean(),
     "remainder": (remainder["SHOT_TYPE"] == "3PT Field Goal").mean(), "test": "chi-square", "p_value": chi2_p("SHOT_TYPE")},
    {"variable": "ACTION_TYPE mix (top 20 + other)", "sample": np.nan, "remainder": np.nan, "test": "chi-square", "p_value": chi2_p("ACTION_TYPE")},
    {"variable": "SHOT_ZONE_BASIC mix", "sample": np.nan, "remainder": np.nan, "test": "chi-square", "p_value": chi2_p("SHOT_ZONE_BASIC")},
    {"variable": "SHOT_ZONE_AREA mix", "sample": np.nan, "remainder": np.nan, "test": "chi-square", "p_value": chi2_p("SHOT_ZONE_AREA")},
    {"variable": "overtime share", "sample": sample["PERIOD"].gt(4).mean(), "remainder": remainder["PERIOD"].gt(4).mean(),
     "test": "chi-square", "p_value": chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(np.r_[np.zeros(len(sample)), np.ones(len(remainder))],
                                                                    np.r_[sample["PERIOD"].gt(4), remainder["PERIOD"].gt(4)]))[1]},
]).set_index("variable").round(4)
check.to_csv(REP / "sample_representativeness.csv"); display(check)

Representativeness. FG% and season shares match the population by design, because they are the strata, so they are not evidence. The real test compares the sample with the unsampled remainder (832k shots, an independent group) on variables that were not stratified on. No test finds a difference:

  • shot distance (KS p = 0.99) and horizontal location (p = 0.45);
  • 3-point share (χ² p = 0.37) and overtime share (p = 0.86);
  • the mix of shot types (ACTION_TYPE, p = 0.85) and of court zones (p = 0.70 and 0.57).

Because the sampling is proportional, the base rate is not distorted, which matters because the model must output real probabilities. Per-stratum rounding gives 199,999 shots instead of 200,000.

In [5]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit

# Split by GAME_ID: shots from the same game never sit in two partitions. This guards against within-game
# correlation only; player-level correlation (the same shooter in all partitions) remains - acceptable because
# shooter identity is not a model input, and the out-of-time season is the real test of generalisation.
tr_frac, va_frac, te_frac = PARTITION
idx_train, idx_rest = next(GroupShuffleSplit(1, test_size=va_frac + te_frac, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
                           .split(sample, groups=sample["GAME_ID"]))
rest = sample.iloc[idx_rest]
idx_val, idx_test = next(GroupShuffleSplit(1, test_size=te_frac / (va_frac + te_frac), random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
                         .split(rest, groups=rest["GAME_ID"]))
train, valid, test = sample.iloc[idx_train], rest.iloc[idx_val], rest.iloc[idx_test]
partitions = pd.DataFrame({p: {"shots": len(d), "games": d["GAME_ID"].nunique(), "FG%": round(d[TARGET].mean(), 4),
                               **{f"share {s}": round((d["SEASON"] == s).mean(), 3) for s in sorted(sample["SEASON"].unique())}}
                           for p, d in [("train", train), ("validate", valid), ("test", test)]}).T
partitions.to_csv(REP / "data_partition.csv"); display(partitions)
g_tr, g_va, g_te = set(train.GAME_ID), set(valid.GAME_ID), set(test.GAME_ID)
assert not (g_tr & g_va) and not (g_tr & g_te) and not (g_va & g_te), "a game appears in two partitions"

# Is SAMPLE_SIZE big enough? Learning curve: validation log loss vs. number of training shots. Extra training shots
# beyond the 120k training partition come from population games that are in neither validation nor test.
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, log_loss

quick = lambda d: d[["LOC_X", "LOC_Y", "PERIOD", "MINUTES_REMAINING", "SECONDS_REMAINING"]].assign(
    action=d["ACTION_TYPE"].cat.codes)
pool = population[~population["GAME_ID"].isin(g_va | g_te)]
curve = []
for n in [2_000, 5_000, 10_000, 25_000, 50_000, 120_000, 240_000, 480_000]:
    sub = pool.sample(n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=500, early_stopping=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(quick(sub), sub[TARGET])
    p = m.predict_proba(quick(valid))[:, 1]
    curve.append({"train_shots": n, "val_auc": roc_auc_score(valid[TARGET], p), "val_log_loss": log_loss(valid[TARGET], p)})
curve = pd.DataFrame(curve).round(4); curve.to_csv(REP / "learning_curve.csv", index=False); display(curve)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
curve.plot(x="train_shots", y="val_log_loss", marker="o", logx=True, legend=False, ax=ax, title="Learning curve (lower log loss = better)")
ax.axvline(len(train), c="gray", ls="--"); ax.set_ylabel("validation log loss"); savefig("sample_learning_curve")
train_shots val_auc val_log_loss
0 2000 0.6338 0.6563
1 5000 0.6359 0.6524
2 10000 0.6393 0.6470
3 25000 0.6512 0.6396
4 50000 0.6580 0.6369
5 120000 0.6620 0.6351
6 240000 0.6636 0.6344
7 480000 0.6650 0.6338

Is the sample big enough? The learning curve now uses early stopping (so small samples are not just over-fitted). It extends past the 120k training partition with extra shots from population games that sit in neither validation nor test. Validation log loss falls quickly up to ~25k shots (0.656 → 0.640), then slowly: 0.6351 at 120k, 0.6344 at 240k, 0.6338 at 480k. The last 360k shots buy 0.0013. That is not nothing: it is about the size of the gap between the top models in A.1. So the 200k sample is enough to compare model families, which is SEMMA's argument for sampling. The model that is deployed is then refit on train + validate (160k shots) to use more of the data.

Partitioning. Train/validate/test = 60/20/20 grouped by game (3,497 / 1,166 / 1,166 games), so shots from one game never sit in two partitions. FG% is 46.9 / 46.8 / 46.4 %, and season shares per partition are within 3 points of each other. Grouping by game guards against within-game correlation only. The same players and teams still appear in all three partitions. That is acceptable because shooter and team identity are not inputs, and the out-of-time 2024-25 season (new games, a new year) is the real test of generalisation.

Output of Sample: a stratified, representative 200k-shot sample; three game-grouped partitions; plus the full 2024-25 season held back for an out-of-time check in Assess.

🔍 Critic review — Sample¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the SEMMA data mining methodology and SAS Enterprise Miner, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on SEMMA and predictive modeling. Review the Sample phase of my NBA expected-field-goal-percentage project below. Check it against everything SEMMA's Sample step should accomplish (and the Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it). Focus especially on: whether the sample is demonstrably representative, whether the sample size is justified, whether the partitioning prevents leakage (grouping by game, out-of-time hold-out), and whether stratification choices are explained. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Learning curve uses a reduced feature set, so it only indicates the needed size; stratifying on the target needs justification; two atypical seasons. Stated as indicative (flat after ~25k shots, so 200k has a wide margin); showed proportional stratification keeps FG% exactly; checked season FG% (46.0–47.5 %).
2 Representativeness evidence circular (stratified variables; KS against its own population); learning curve too short. (B overall) Tests against the unsampled remainder on unstratified variables; learning curve to 480k shots; deployed model refit on 160k.
3 Sound; minor wording on the partition. (B+ overall) No further change needed.

Findings.

  • EVENT_TYPE ("Made Shot"/"Missed Shot") matches the target perfectly (56,283 makes, 63,731 misses, zero disagreements). It is the target in disguise and must be dropped.
  • GRID_TYPE and SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG are constant, and there are no missing values in any of the 25 columns.
  • Shots cluster at the rim (30 % in the restricted area) and beyond the arc (39 % threes); Jump Shot alone is 32 % of attempts.

Anomalies:

  • 251 shots come from beyond half court (FG 3.6 %) and 229 are logged in the backcourt zone (2.6 %). These are real end-of-quarter heaves, kept and flagged by the heave variable.
  • 2,105 shots (1.75 %) have LOC_Y below the hoop line. They are baseline shots under and behind the rim (FG 42.8 %), also real.
  • Only 2 of the 48 ACTION_TYPE labels are missing from some season (0.12 % of shots), so the label set is stable across seasons. ACTION_TYPE is assigned by the scorer after the play, so a missed dunk could be logged as a layup. Whether that happens cannot be checked without video, but its consequence can be measured: A.1 fits the champion without the shot-type label.

E.3 Variable Selection (variable worth)¶

In [11]:
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
cand = train.drop(columns=[TARGET, "EVENT_TYPE", "GRID_TYPE", "SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG"] + ID_COLS)
s = cand.sample(30_000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
enc = s.apply(lambda c: c.cat.codes if hasattr(c, "cat") else c)
discrete = [hasattr(cand[c], "cat") or cand[c].nunique() < 20 for c in enc.columns]
mi = pd.Series(mutual_info_classif(enc, train.loc[s.index, TARGET], discrete_features=discrete, random_state=RANDOM_STATE), index=enc.columns)
# Plug-in MI on a discrete variable with K levels is biased upward by about (K - 1) / (2N) nats (Miller-Madow);
# without the correction a variable with hundreds of levels (PLAYER_NAME) looks informative just because it has many levels.
bias = pd.Series({c: (s[c].nunique() - 1) / (2 * len(s)) if d else 0.0 for c, d in zip(enc.columns, discrete)})
worth = pd.DataFrame({"mutual_information": mi, "small_sample_bias": bias, "corrected_MI": (mi - bias).clip(lower=0),
                      "levels": s.nunique()}).sort_values("corrected_MI", ascending=False)
worth.round(5).to_csv(REP / "variable_worth.csv"); display(worth.round(4))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
worth["corrected_MI"].sort_values().plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#4C72B0", title="Variable worth: bias-corrected mutual information with SHOT_MADE_FLAG")
ax.set_xlabel("nats"); savefig("explore_variable_worth")

Variable worth.

  • Shot type (ACTION_TYPE, MI 0.042) and distance (SHOT_DISTANCE 0.034, zone 0.030, LOC_Y 0.024, LOC_X 0.023) carry the most information.
  • Mutual information on a variable with many levels is biased upward. For PLAYER_NAME (806 levels in the sample) the bias is 0.013 of its raw 0.022, so after the correction shooter identity carries only 0.008. It is excluded by design anyway: this model measures shot quality, and who made the shot is analysed afterwards (A.4) as shot making.
  • Game-clock fields carry almost nothing on their own (≤ 0.0002) but matter in one situation, end-of-quarter heaves (E.2).
  • Distance is represented several overlapping ways (distance, zone, range, location). Modify replaces them with one consistent geometry.

Exploration findings¶

# Finding (training partition) Implication for Modify / Model
1 FG% falls fastest right at the rim: 76 % at 0 ft, 71 % at 1 ft, 59 % at 2 ft, 48 % at 3 ft, 41 % at 5 ft. It stays flat at about 43 % through mid-range (10–15 ft), drops to about 36 % at the arc, 31 % at 30 ft, 23 % at 33 ft and 17 % at 35 ft strongly non-linear distance effect → fine distance bins near the rim plus a log distance for the regression; trees handle it natively
2 Corner threes go in more than above-the-break threes, partly because they are shorter (22–23 ft vs 24–25 ft). At the same integer distance of 24 ft the gap shrinks to 37.0 % vs 35.2 % (n = 1,474 vs 4,893) a corner-three flag; the shot angle is tested in Model (it adds nothing measurable)
3 Shot type matters as much as location: dunks 89 %, layups 56 %, floaters 45 %, pull-ups 40 %, jump shots 37 %. Rare labels (e.g. "Running Alley Oop Dunk Shot") are too small to model alone keep ACTION_TYPE; add a shot family so rare labels are pooled with shots of the same kind
4 Late-clock shots go in less at every distance: with ≤ 3 s left, 49 % (0–10 ft) and 8 % (30+ ft), against 57 % and 33 % with more than 24 s left add the seconds left and a heave flag (≤ 3 s and ≥ 30 ft). No finding supports a separate clutch or overtime flag, so neither is used
5 K-means on location finds one rim cluster (60 % FG, 2 ft), two mid-range clusters (42–44 %), two corner/short-three clusters (≈ 39 %) and three above-the-break clusters (35–37 %). The clusters are descriptive only and are not used as inputs consistent with finding 2
6 Anomalies: heaves from beyond half court and the backcourt (0.4 % of shots), baseline shots behind the hoop line (1.75 %) keep: all real shots; the heave flag covers the first group
⚠ EVENT_TYPE duplicates the target; GRID_TYPE, SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG constant drop

🔍 Critic review — Explore¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the SEMMA data mining methodology and SAS Enterprise Miner, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on SEMMA and predictive modeling. Review the Explore phase of my NBA expected-field-goal-percentage project below. Check it against everything SEMMA's Explore step should accomplish (and the Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it). Focus especially on: whether exploration used only the training partition, whether findings are quantified and translated into concrete Modify actions, and whether leakage and redundant variables were detected. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Player identity has high variable worth but is dropped without argument; clusters are only descriptive. Explained the shot-quality vs shot-making design choice; linked clusters to the angle/corner variables.
2 Variable-worth figure corrupted; plug-in MI inflated PLAYER_NAME; anomalies and redundancy not analysed. Figure fixed; bias-corrected MI (PLAYER_NAME 0.022 → 0.008); anomaly table; label stability by season.
3 "Matched-distance" corner comparison not matched; ACTION_TYPE risk declared untestable; no redundancy matrix. Comparison at exactly 24 ft (37.0 % vs 35.2 %); correlation matrix of engineered inputs; label risk measured by ablation in Model.

M — Modify¶

Goal: create, select and transform variables to focus the model-building process. Every transformation is written as score code — a small Python module reused unchanged by the deployed app, the equivalent of Enterprise Miner's exported score code.

M.2 Transform Variables · Replacement · Interactive Binning — as score code¶

In [14]:
SCORE_CODE = r"""
# Score code for the NBA xFG% model: the Modify step, shared by the notebook and the app.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_INPUTS = ["LOC_X", "LOC_Y", "ACTION_TYPE", "PERIOD", "MINUTES_REMAINING", "SECONDS_REMAINING"]
NUMERIC = ["dist_ft", "log_dist", "abs_angle", "is_three", "is_corner_three", "secs_left_period", "PERIOD", "heave"]
CATEGORICAL = ["action", "action_family", "distance_bin"]
# finer bins near the rim, where FG% falls fastest (Explore finding 1)
BIN_EDGES = [-0.1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 16, 23.75, 30, 100]
BIN_LABELS = ["0-1 ft", "1-2 ft", "2-3 ft", "3-5 ft", "5-10 ft", "10-16 ft", "16-23.75 ft", "23.75-30 ft", "30+ ft"]


def action_family(action):
    # Group the scorer's ACTION_TYPE labels into shot families, so rare labels (e.g. 'Running Alley Oop Dunk Shot')
    # are still recognised as what they are instead of being pooled with unrelated rare shots.
    if pd.isna(action):
        return np.nan
    a = str(action).lower()
    for family, keys in [("dunk", ["dunk"]), ("tip/putback", ["tip", "putback"]), ("alley-oop", ["alley oop"]),
                         ("layup", ["layup", "finger roll"]), ("hook", ["hook"]), ("floater", ["float"]),
                         ("bank shot", ["bank"]), ("fadeaway/turnaround", ["fadeaway", "turnaround"]),
                         ("pull-up/step-back", ["pull", "step back"]), ("jump shot", ["jump"])]:
        if any(k in a for k in keys):
            return family
    return "other"


def engineer(raw):
    # Transform raw shot records (RAW_INPUTS) into model inputs. Stateless, so it is safe to reuse anywhere.
    # Missing inputs stay missing (NaN) so the Impute step in the pipeline can handle them.
    d = pd.DataFrame(raw).copy()
    num = lambda c: pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors="coerce")
    x, y = num("LOC_X"), num("LOC_Y")                               # tenths of feet, hoop at (0, 0)
    has_loc = x.notna() & y.notna()
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=d.index)
    out["dist_ft"] = np.hypot(x, y) / 10
    out["log_dist"] = np.log1p(out["dist_ft"])
    out["abs_angle"] = np.degrees(np.arctan2(x, y)).abs()            # 0 = straight on, 90 = along the baseline
    corner = (x.abs() >= 220) & (y <= 92.5)
    out["is_corner_three"] = corner.astype(float).where(has_loc)
    out["is_three"] = (corner | (np.hypot(x, y) >= 237.5)).astype(float).where(has_loc)
    out["secs_left_period"] = num("MINUTES_REMAINING") * 60 + num("SECONDS_REMAINING")
    out["PERIOD"] = num("PERIOD")
    out["heave"] = ((out["secs_left_period"] <= 3) & (out["dist_ft"] >= 30)).astype(float).where(
        out["secs_left_period"].notna() & has_loc)
    out["action"] = d["ACTION_TYPE"].astype(object).where(d["ACTION_TYPE"].notna(), np.nan)
    out["action_family"] = out["action"].map(action_family)
    out["distance_bin"] = pd.cut(out["dist_ft"], BIN_EDGES, labels=BIN_LABELS).astype(object)
    out["distance_bin"] = out["distance_bin"].where(out["dist_ft"].notna(), np.nan)
    return out[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL]


class AveragedModel:
    # Ensemble node: averages the predicted probabilities of already-fitted pipelines.
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.models = models
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        p = np.mean([m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] for m in self.models], axis=0)
        return np.column_stack([1 - p, p])

    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)
"""
(APP / "shot_features.py").write_text(SCORE_CODE.lstrip(), encoding="utf-8")
if str(APP) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(APP))
import importlib, shot_features
importlib.reload(shot_features)

print(f"Geometry-based 3PT flag agrees with the official SHOT_TYPE on {agree:.2%} of training shots")
fam = train.assign(family=train["ACTION_TYPE"].map(action_family)).groupby("family")[TARGET].agg(shots="size", FG_pct="mean")
display(fam.sort_values("FG_pct", ascending=False).round(3).T)

M.3 Replacement & Impute (inside the model pipeline)¶

Rare action labels (< 0.5 % of training shots) are replaced by a pooled "infrequent" level, but each keeps its shot family through action_family. The pooling applies to the raw label only; all 10 families and all distance bins are kept, and an unseen family or bin is simply ignored. The 19 pooled labels are 6 dunks, 5 bank shots, 3 layups, 3 hooks and 2 alley-oops, so a rare dunk is still scored as a dunk. Missing values (none in training, but possible in new data) stay missing through the score code and are imputed in the pipeline; the probes confirm that a shot with missing location, clock and shot type is scored (xFG 0.55, close to the league average), and an unseen label is still scored by its family ("Spinning Reverse Dunk Shot" at the rim: 0.92). Both steps are learned from the training partition only.

Changes made after review:

  • finer distance bins at the rim (0–1, 1–2, 2–3, 3–5 ft) and a log distance, following finding 1;
  • one angle representation (abs_angle) instead of two;
  • the clutch and is_overtime flags removed, because no Explore finding supported them.

Redundancy (table above): distance appears as dist_ft, log_dist (r = 0.95), is_three (0.88) and the distance bins. That is harmless for the tree models. For the regression it means the coefficients are identified only by the L2 penalty, which is why they are read only for direction.

In [16]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

def make_prep(numeric=NUMERIC, use_action=True):
    # Rare-level Replacement applies to the raw scorer label only; shot family and distance bin keep every level
    # (an unseen value is simply ignored rather than mapped to some pooled level).
    impute_cat = lambda: SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing")
    parts = [("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), list(numeric))]
    if use_action:
        parts += [("act", Pipeline([("impute", impute_cat()), ("replace_rare", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                                                                                              min_frequency=0.005, sparse_output=False))]), ["action"]),
                  ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", impute_cat()), ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]),
                   ["action_family", "distance_bin"])]
    else:
        parts += [("cat", Pipeline([("impute", impute_cat()), ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]), ["distance_bin"])]
    return ColumnTransformer(parts)

prep_preview = make_prep().fit(engineer(train))
names = prep_preview.get_feature_names_out()
pooled = prep_preview.named_transformers_["act"].named_steps["replace_rare"].infrequent_categories_[0]
print(f"{len(names)} model inputs after Replacement/one-hot. {len(pooled)} rare action labels are pooled, "
      f"but each keeps its own shot family through action_family (all {engineer(train)['action_family'].nunique()} families are kept):")
display(pd.Series({a: action_family(a) for a in pooled}).value_counts().to_frame("rare labels per family").T)
X_tr, X_va, X_te = (d[RAW_INPUTS] for d in (train, valid, test))
y_tr, y_va, y_te = (d[TARGET].to_numpy() for d in (train, valid, test))

🔍 Critic review — Modify¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the SEMMA data mining methodology and SAS Enterprise Miner, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on SEMMA and predictive modeling. Review the Modify phase of my NBA expected-field-goal-percentage project below. Check it against everything SEMMA's Modify step should accomplish (and the Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it). Focus especially on: whether every transformation is justified by an Explore finding, whether anything is fitted on non-training data, whether dropped variables (leakage, identity, redundancy) are correctly reasoned, and whether the score code is reusable at deployment. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 ACTION_TYPE is coded by scorers and could reflect the outcome; verify the geometry-based 3PT flag. Recorded as a limitation (standard in public xFG models); showed 99.95 % agreement of the 3PT flag.
2 Rare-level pooling merged dunks with bank shots; imputation never reached (casts crashed on NaN); unsupported flags. Shot families; NaN-safe score code + probe; finer rim bins and log distance; clutch / overtime flags dropped.
3 Pooling also collapsed the alley-oop family; unseen inputs defaulted to it. Pooling limited to the raw label; families and bins keep every level; probes check the predicted value.

M — Model¶

Goal: let the software search for a combination of inputs that reliably predicts the outcome. Several model families compete; the validation partition is used to tune and compare them (as Enterprise Miner does).

In [17]:

Baseline — zone average¶

In [18]:
# Three baselines, from naive to strong:
#  1) base rate - every shot gets the training FG% (the no-information log loss)
#  2) zone average - the league FG% of the shot's official court zone
#  3) zone x shot family - the same, split by shot family (uses the strongest input, ACTION_TYPE, like the models do)
zone_keys = ["SHOT_ZONE_BASIC", "SHOT_ZONE_AREA", "SHOT_ZONE_RANGE"]
base_rate = train[TARGET].mean()
def group_rate(d, keys, min_shots=30):
    key = lambda f: f[keys].astype(str).agg("|".join, axis=1)
    g = train.assign(k=key(train)).groupby("k")[TARGET].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= min_shots]["mean"]
    return key(d).map(g).to_numpy(dtype=float)
def zone_baseline(d):
    return np.nan_to_num(group_rate(d, zone_keys), nan=base_rate)
def zone_family_baseline(d):
    d = d.assign(family=d["ACTION_TYPE"].map(action_family))
    p = group_rate(d, zone_keys + ["family"]) if "family" in d else None
    return np.where(np.isnan(p), zone_baseline(d), p)
train = train.assign(family=train["ACTION_TYPE"].map(action_family))
val_pred["Baseline: base rate"] = np.full(len(valid), base_rate)
val_pred["Baseline: zone average"] = zone_baseline(valid)
val_pred["Baseline: zone x shot family"] = zone_family_baseline(valid)
for b in ["Baseline: base rate", "Baseline: zone average", "Baseline: zone x shot family"]:
    print(f"{b:<30}", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in scores(y_va, val_pred[b]).items()})

Model families in the competition¶

Node What it is Assumptions / strengths Settings tried on validation → chosen
Base rate every shot gets the training FG% the no-information benchmark (log loss 0.691) —
Zone average league FG% of the official zone no learning beyond the zone; the "analyst's" benchmark —
Zone × shot family league FG% of the zone and shot family a strong benchmark that uses the same key input as the models —
Regression logistic regression on scaled inputs + one-hot shot type, shot family and distance bins linear in log-odds; the bins supply the non-linearity. Overlapping encodings are kept apart only by the L2 penalty, so coefficients show direction (dunk family +0.81, tip layups −0.90, 0–1 ft +0.53 log-odds) rather than clean effects 4 values of C → C = 0.1
Decision Tree single CART tree captures interactions, easy to read; high variance 6 depths → depth 6
Neural Network MLP flexible smooth functions; needs scaled inputs 4 architectures / penalties / learning rates → 16 units, α = 0.01
Gradient Boosting histogram gradient-boosted trees strongest on tabular data; interactions + non-linearity. Early stopping holds back 10 % of training internally 4 settings → learning rate 0.08, 31 leaves, 60 iterations
Ensemble average of regression, NN and boosting probabilities reduces variance if the members disagree; the tree is left out as the weakest learner —

🔍 Critic review — Model¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the SEMMA data mining methodology and SAS Enterprise Miner, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on SEMMA and predictive modeling. Review the Model phase of my NBA expected-field-goal-percentage project below. Check it against everything SEMMA's Model step should accomplish (and the Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it). Focus especially on: whether the competing model families are well chosen and fairly configured, whether tuning used only the validation partition, whether a meaningful baseline is included, and whether settings are documented. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Unfair comparison — the tree was tuned on validation but boosting was not; neural network untuned. Tuned boosting over 4 settings on validation (lr 0.05, 31 leaves); NN left as is (ensemble including it does not beat boosting).
2 Unequal tuning; champion picked on a 0.0006 gap without uncertainty; weak baseline. Every family tuned; game-level paired bootstrap; base-rate and zone × shot-family baselines.
3 No model without the post-hoc shot-type label. Ablations: without the shot type 0.6471 (worse than the zone × family baseline); without the angle no measurable change.

A — Assess¶

Goal: evaluate the usefulness and reliability of the findings — compare models, check calibration, confirm on untouched data, and score new data.

A.1 Model Comparison (validation partition)¶

In [24]:
comparison = pd.DataFrame({m: scores(y_va, p) for m, p in val_pred.items()}).T
comparison["settings_tried"] = pd.Series(search_size)
comparison["fit_seconds"] = pd.Series(fit_secs).round(1)

CHAMPION = comparison.drop(index=[i for i in comparison.index if i.startswith(("Baseline", "Ablation"))]).index[0]

# Are the differences bigger than noise? Paired bootstrap over GAMES of the validation partition (shots in a game
# are not independent): 95 % interval of each model's log-loss difference against the champion.
games = valid["GAME_ID"].to_numpy(); ug, ginv = np.unique(games, return_inverse=True)
shot_ll = lambda p: -(y_va * np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1)) + (1 - y_va) * np.log(np.clip(1 - p, 1e-12, 1)))
game_sum = lambda v: np.bincount(ginv, weights=v, minlength=len(ug))
n_shots = np.bincount(ginv, minlength=len(ug)); champ_ll = game_sum(shot_ll(val_pred[CHAMPION]))
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE); boot_idx = rng.integers(0, len(ug), (1000, len(ug)))
paired = []
for m, p in val_pred.items():
    if m == CHAMPION: continue
    d = game_sum(shot_ll(p)) - champ_ll
    diffs = d[boot_idx].sum(1) / n_shots[boot_idx].sum(1)
    paired.append({"model": m, "log_loss_minus_champion": d.sum() / n_shots.sum(),
                   "ci_95_low": np.quantile(diffs, .025), "ci_95_high": np.quantile(diffs, .975)})
paired = pd.DataFrame(paired).set_index("model").sort_values("log_loss_minus_champion").round(5)
paired["clearly_worse"] = paired["ci_95_low"] > 0
paired.to_csv(REP / "model_comparison_bootstrap.csv"); display(paired)
print(f"Champion (lowest validation log loss): {CHAMPION} | models not clearly worse: {paired.index[~paired['clearly_worse']].tolist()}")

Why log loss? xFG% is used as a probability (expected points = xFG% × shot value), so the selection criterion must reward accurate probabilities — not just ranking (AUC) or a 50 % cutoff (accuracy). Brier score agrees with log loss on the ranking of every model.

Result. Gradient boosting has the lowest validation log loss (0.6338). A paired bootstrap over the 1,166 validation games shows it is statistically tied with the ensemble (difference +0.0001, 95 % CI −0.0003 to +0.0005). Boosting is kept as champion because it is a single, simpler model. The neural network (+0.0012), regression (+0.0020) and the tree (+0.0033) are clearly worse.

Every learned model beats all three baselines: the zone average (0.6573), the stronger zone × shot-family average (0.6454) and the base rate (0.6910). The champion's honest gain over the strong baseline is 0.0116 log loss (1.8 %, CI 0.0100–0.0131), and AUC rises from 0.647 to 0.666. The gain looks modest because most of a shot's outcome is genuinely random once you know only where and what it was; the model cannot see the defender, the shooter's balance or the pass.

The champion relies on vertical location (shuffling it raises log loss by 0.043), shot type (0.039) and horizontal location (0.037); the game clock adds about 0.001.

Ablations (not candidates for champion):

  • Without the shot-type label (location + clock only), the same boosting configuration scores 0.6471. That is clearly worse than the champion (+0.0132) and even worse than the zone × shot-family baseline. So most of the model's edge comes from the scorer's shot-type label. That label is recorded after the play: if scorers sometimes log a missed dunk as a layup, part of this gain is leakage. The location-only model's gain over the zone average (0.0102) is free of that risk.
  • Without the shot angle, it scores 0.6340: no measurable difference (CI −0.0001 to +0.0004). The angle is kept because it is harmless for trees, but it adds nothing beyond distance and the corner flag. Its top-rated 10 % of shots go in about 1.8 times as often as average.

# What does the champion rely on? Permutation importance of the six raw inputs (validation, log-loss scoring)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
sub = X_va.sample(10_000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
pi = permutation_importance(fitted[CHAMPION], sub, y_va[X_va.index.get_indexer(sub.index)], scoring="neg_log_loss",
                            n_repeats=3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
display(pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=RAW_INPUTS).sort_values(ascending=False).round(4).to_frame("increase in log loss when shuffled"))

# Calibration on the unseen 2024-25 season: by decile, and by segment (zone, 2PT/3PT, shot family).
# Player rankings depend on calibration WITHIN shot types, which a decile table cannot show.
y_oot, p_oot = final[list(final)[-1]][:2]
cal = pd.DataFrame({"xFG": p_oot, "made": y_oot})
cal["decile"] = pd.qcut(cal["xFG"], 10, labels=[f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 11)])
cal = cal.groupby("decile", observed=True).agg(shots=("made", "size"), mean_xFG=("xFG", "mean"), actual_FG=("made", "mean"))
cal["gap_pct_points"] = (cal["actual_FG"] - cal["mean_xFG"]) * 100
cal = cal.round(3); cal.to_csv(REP / "calibration_by_decile_2024_25.csv"); display(cal)

No over-fitting, and it travels to a new season.

  • Over-fitting. Training log loss (0.6320) is only slightly below validation (0.6338) and test (0.6339), so the model does not memorise its training shots. Test equals validation, so choosing the champion on validation did not over-fit either.
  • New season. On the full 2024-25 season, which the model never saw, log loss is 0.6370 against 0.6466 for the zone × family baseline and 0.6577 for the zone baseline, and AUC is 0.659: a small, expected decline.
  • Calibration in the large. Predicted 46.5 % vs actual 46.7 %.
  • Calibration by decile. Every gap is ≤ 1.5 percentage points (largest in D7: 44.4 % predicted, 45.9 % actual).
  • Calibration by segment. Every shot zone and shot family with 500+ shots is within 2.1 points, with one exception: backcourt heaves (517 shots) are over-predicted, 7.2 % vs 2.3 %. Two systematic gaps matter for players: layups go in 2.1 points more than predicted and pull-ups 1.2 points less. Players who live at the rim are therefore slightly flattered by the leaderboard in A.4, and pull-up shooters slightly penalised.

The three success criteria are met.

Process note: the test partition and the 2024-25 season were never used to fit or choose anything. But their results were visible in every review round while the analysis was revised (rim bins, shot families, extra baselines). "Unseen" therefore holds for training, not for model development. The effect is likely small, because test still equals validation.

# Shot making over expected, 2024-25. Players are grouped by PLAYER_ID (names are spelled with and without accents in
# different seasons). Points come from the OFFICIAL shot type. Each player gets a 95 % interval (binomial, given the xFG of
# his own shots) and an empirical-Bayes estimate shrunk towards the group mean (high-volume shooters are above average).
oot = oot.assign(xFG=p_oot, pts=np.where(oot["SHOT_TYPE"] == "3PT Field Goal", 3, 2))
players = oot.groupby("PLAYER_ID").agg(PLAYER_NAME=("PLAYER_NAME", lambda s: str(s.iloc[-1])), team=("TEAM_NAME", lambda s: s.mode()[0]),
                                       FGA=(TARGET, "size"), FG_pct=(TARGET, "mean"), xFG_pct=("xFG", "mean"),
                                       var_sum=("xFG", lambda s: (s * (1 - s)).sum()),
                                       points=(TARGET, lambda s: (s * oot.loc[s.index, "pts"]).sum()),
                                       expected_points=("xFG", lambda s: (s * oot.loc[s.index, "pts"]).sum()))
players = players[players["FGA"] >= 500].assign(FG_over_expected=lambda d: d["FG_pct"] - d["xFG_pct"],
                                                points_over_expected=lambda d: d["points"] - d["expected_points"],
                                                se=lambda d: np.sqrt(d["var_sum"]) / d["FGA"])
mu = players["FG_over_expected"].mean()
true_var = max(players["FG_over_expected"].var() - (players["se"] ** 2).mean(), 0)      # spread of real differences
players["FGOE_shrunk"] = mu + (players["FG_over_expected"] - mu) * true_var / (true_var + players["se"] ** 2)
players["ci_95_low"], players["ci_95_high"] = players["FG_over_expected"] - 1.96 * players["se"], players["FG_over_expected"] + 1.96 * players["se"]
players["clearly_above_or_below_0"] = (players["ci_95_low"] > 0) | (players["ci_95_high"] < 0)
players = players.drop(columns="var_sum").reset_index().set_index("PLAYER_NAME").sort_values("points_over_expected", ascending=False).round(3)
players.to_csv(REP / "shot_making_leaderboard_2024_25.csv")
print(f"{len(players)} players with 500+ FGA in {oot['SEASON'].iloc[0]}; group mean FG over expected {mu * 100:+.1f} pts; "
      f"typical 95 % interval ±{1.96 * players['se'].median() * 100:.1f} pts; {players['clearly_above_or_below_0'].sum()} players clearly "
      f"different from 0 (about {0.05 * len(players):.0f} would be by chance)")
display(players.head(15)); display(players.tail(5))

# Is "FG over expected" persistent? Compare 2023-24 with 2024-25 for the same PLAYER_ID, and benchmark against how much raw
# FG% and the xFG% of a player's shots persist on their own. Persistence alone cannot separate shot-making skill from
# shot context the model does not see (defender distance, self-created vs assisted) that is stable for a player's role.
prev = population[population["SEASON"] == "2023-24"]
prev = prev.assign(xFG=champ.predict_proba(prev[RAW_INPUTS])[:, 1])
prev_players = prev.groupby("PLAYER_ID").agg(FGA=(TARGET, "size"), FG_pct=(TARGET, "mean"), xFG_pct=("xFG", "mean"))
prev_players = prev_players[prev_players["FGA"] >= 500].assign(FG_over_expected=lambda d: d["FG_pct"] - d["xFG_pct"])
both = players.reset_index().set_index("PLAYER_ID")[["PLAYER_NAME", "FG_over_expected", "FG_pct", "xFG_pct"]].join(
    prev_players[["FG_over_expected", "FG_pct", "xFG_pct"]], how="inner", rsuffix="_2023_24")
def r_ci(a, b):
    r = np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1]; z, se = np.arctanh(r), 1 / np.sqrt(len(a) - 3)
    return r, np.tanh(z - 1.96 * se), np.tanh(z + 1.96 * se)
persistence = pd.DataFrame([dict(zip(["r", "ci_95_low", "ci_95_high"], r_ci(both[m], both[f"{m}_2023_24"])), measure=m)
                            for m in ["FG_over_expected", "FG_pct", "xFG_pct"]]).set_index("measure").round(2)
both.to_csv(REP / "shot_making_persistence.csv"); persistence.to_csv(REP / "shot_making_persistence_summary.csv")
r = persistence.loc["FG_over_expected", "r"]

Reading the chart: above the diagonal = the player makes more than his shots would predict (shot making); further right = he takes higher-quality shots (shot selection). With about 1,000 attempts, a player's FG over expected has a 95 % interval of about ±3.3 points. 62 of the 181 players are clearly different from zero (about 9 would be by chance alone), and the rest are within noise. The leaderboard also shows an empirical-Bayes shrunk estimate that pulls noisy players towards the group mean (+0.7 points: players with 500+ attempts are, as a group, better than average).

  • Nikola Jokić leads by far: 57.6 % on shots worth 46.6 %, +327 points over expected (FG over expected +11.0 points, 95 % CI +8.5 to +13.6; shrunk +9.3). His shots are not unusually easy; he simply converts them.
  • Kevin Durant (+226) takes clearly harder shots (xFG 43.7 %) and still makes 52.7 % of them. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is +196.
  • Stephen Curry's xFG% is low (40.4 %) because of his shot diet (long threes), yet he is +139: raw FG% (44.8 %) badly undersells him.
  • At the bottom: Stephon Castle (−138), Alex Sarr (−137), Keon Johnson (−114), Bilal Coulibaly (−109) and Scottie Barnes (−91). Three of the five are in their first or second NBA season.

Skill, or a persistent residual? For the 131 players with 500+ attempts in both 2023-24 and 2024-25 (matched by player ID; names are spelled with and without accents in different seasons):

  • FG over expected correlates r = 0.70 across seasons (95 % CI 0.60–0.78);
  • raw FG% correlates more (r = 0.86), and the xFG% of a player's shots most of all (0.94).

Shot diet is very stable, and shot-making-over-expected persists moderately. It can only be called a persistent residual: real shot-making skill plus shot context the model cannot see but that is stable for a player's role (defender distance, self-created vs assisted, post-ups). The sample also keeps only players who held a big role in both seasons. And 2023-24 xFG is partly in-sample: about 12 % of those shots were training data, which slightly flatters that season.

What the model does not know: defender distance, catch-and-shoot vs off-the-dribble beyond the ACTION_TYPE label, fatigue, and play context. Player-tracking data would close much of that gap, but it is not public.

🔍 Critic review — Assess¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the SEMMA data mining methodology and SAS Enterprise Miner, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on SEMMA and predictive modeling. Review the Assess phase of my NBA expected-field-goal-percentage project below. Check it against everything SEMMA's Assess step should accomplish (and the Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it). Focus especially on: whether the champion was selected on an appropriate criterion, whether the test partition and out-of-time season were used only once, whether calibration was checked, and whether the player-level findings are interpreted with appropriate caveats. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Calibration only checked on average; the leaderboard could be noise; explain the modest AUC gain. Added decile calibration on 2024-25 (all gaps ≤ 0.9 pts); added season-to-season persistence check (r = 0.68); explained irreducible randomness and log-loss gain.
2 "Repeatable skill" overclaimed; only decile calibration; no player uncertainty; deployment unfinished; SAS export kept the target leak. Persistence benchmarked; segment calibration; player CIs and shrinkage; refit for deployment; SAS export fixed.
3 Seasons joined on player names (accents differ) → Jokić and 6 others dropped; shrinkage toward 0; SAS partition step wrong. Joined on PLAYER_ID (131 players, r = 0.70); shrinkage toward the group mean; three role-tagged SAS files; full disclosure of hold-out exposure.

Beyond SEMMA — Deployment¶

SEMMA stops at Assess (scoring is part of it); the assignment requires delivery all the way to deployment. The champion configuration is refit on train + validate (160,078 shots, as the learning curve suggests more data helps a little). It is checked once on 2024-25 (log loss 0.6370, the same as the assessed model) and published as a small web app: pick a spot on the court and a shot type → expected FG% and expected points, plus the 2024-25 shot-making leaderboard with 95 % intervals.

APP_CODE = r"""
import json
from pathlib import Path
import joblib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st
from matplotlib.patches import Arc, Circle, Rectangle
from shot_features import engineer   # score code - must sit next to this file

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
st.set_page_config(page_title="NBA xFG%", page_icon="🏀")

@st.cache_resource
def load():
    return joblib.load(HERE / "model.joblib"), json.loads((HERE / "model_metadata.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

model, meta = load()
st.title("🏀 NBA expected field-goal %")
st.caption(f"{meta['champion']} · trained on {meta['trained_on']}")

def court(ax):
    for p in [Circle((0, 0), 7.5, fill=False), Rectangle((-80, -47.5), 160, 190, fill=False),
              Arc((0, 142.5), 120, 120, theta1=0, theta2=180), Arc((0, 0), 80, 80, theta1=0, theta2=180),
              Rectangle((-220, -47.5), 0, 140), Rectangle((220, -47.5), 0, 140), Arc((0, 0), 475, 475, theta1=22, theta2=158),
              Rectangle((-250, -47.5), 500, 470, fill=False)]:
        p.set_edgecolor("#555"); ax.add_patch(p)
    ax.set_xlim(-250, 250); ax.set_ylim(-47.5, 422.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

shot, board = st.tabs(["Evaluate a shot", "2024-25 shot-making leaderboard"])
with shot:
    left, right = st.columns([1, 1])
    with left:
        x_ft = st.slider("Feet left (-) / right (+) of the hoop", -25.0, 25.0, 0.0, 0.5)
        y_ft = st.slider("Feet out from the hoop", -4.0, 40.0, 15.0, 0.5)
        action = st.selectbox("Shot type", meta["actions"], index=0)
        period = st.selectbox("Period", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], index=0, format_func=lambda p: f"Q{p}" if p <= 4 else "OT")
        max_min = 12 if period <= 4 else 5
        minutes = st.number_input("Minutes left in period", 0, max_min, min(6, max_min))
        seconds = st.number_input("Seconds", 0, 59, 0) if minutes < max_min else 0
    raw = pd.DataFrame([{"LOC_X": x_ft * 10, "LOC_Y": y_ft * 10, "ACTION_TYPE": action, "PERIOD": period,
                         "MINUTES_REMAINING": minutes, "SECONDS_REMAINING": seconds}])
    feats = engineer(raw).iloc[0]
    xfg = float(model.predict_proba(raw)[0, 1])
    value = 3 if feats["is_three"] else 2
    with right:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4))
        court(ax); ax.scatter([x_ft * 10], [y_ft * 10], s=120, c="#E4572E", zorder=5)
        st.pyplot(fig)
    c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
    c1.metric("Expected FG%", f"{xfg:.1%}")
    c2.metric("Shot value", f"{value} pts" + (" (corner)" if feats["is_corner_three"] else ""))
    c3.metric("Expected points", f"{xfg * value:.2f}")
    st.caption(f"Distance {feats['dist_ft']:.1f} ft · {feats['abs_angle']:.0f}° from straight-on · shot family: {feats['action_family']}")
    n_support = meta["support"].get(f"{feats['action_family']}|{feats['distance_bin']}", 0)
    if n_support < 30:
        st.warning(f"Unusual shot: only {n_support} training shots of this family at this distance - treat the estimate with caution.")
with board:
    lb = pd.read_csv(HERE / "leaderboard.csv")
    st.write("Players with 500+ attempts. **Points over expected** = actual points from field goals minus the points "
             "an average shooter would score on the same shots. The 95 % interval shows how much of the gap could be luck; "
             "**shrunk** pulls noisy estimates towards zero.")
    st.dataframe(lb[["PLAYER_NAME", "team", "FGA", "FG_pct", "xFG_pct", "FG_over_expected", "ci_95_low", "ci_95_high",
                     "FGOE_shrunk", "points_over_expected"]], hide_index=True)
"""
(APP / "app.py").write_text(APP_CODE.strip() + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
v = meta["versions"]
(APP / "requirements.txt").write_text(f"streamlit>=1.40\nscikit-learn=={v['scikit-learn']}\nnumpy=={v['numpy']}\npandas=={v['pandas']}\njoblib\nmatplotlib\n")
compile(APP_CODE, "app.py", "exec")
print("App files:", sorted(p.name for p in APP.iterdir() if p.is_file()))
print(f"When deploying, choose Python {v['python'][:4]} so the pinned versions install and the model loads.")

Deploy (free): put artifacts/app/ in your GitHub repo → share.streamlit.io → Create app → choose semma/artifacts/app/app.py; under Advanced settings pick the Python version printed above. shot_features.py must stay next to app.py (it is the score code the model was trained with). All library versions are pinned in requirements.txt.

Guard-rails in the app:

  • the shot-type list offers only the 44 labels with at least 50 training shots;
  • the clock cannot exceed 12:00 (5:00 in overtime);
  • the app warns when a shot family / distance combination had fewer than 30 training shots, e.g. a dunk from 25 ft.

Monitoring:

  • each season, compare league-wide mean xFG% with actual FG% (calibration in the large), and re-check calibration by shot zone and shot family;
  • watch for new or retired ACTION_TYPE labels;
  • re-train if a gap exceeds ~1 percentage point overall or ~3 points in a major segment (e.g. after rule changes or new shot trends).

Appendix — SAS Enterprise Miner demo¶

SAS Enterprise Miner is available through SAS OnDemand for Academics when your professor registers the class (SAS Studio alone is free to individuals but has no Enterprise Miner). The cell below exports the exact modeling sample, so the SAS flow uses the same data.

Rebuild the flow in Enterprise Miner:

  1. New project → create a library → import the three files nba_shots_train_for_sas.csv, nba_shots_validate_for_sas.csv and nba_shots_test_for_sas.csv as three data sources.
  2. Input Data / variable roles: SHOT_MADE_FLAG = Target (binary). Set to Rejected every column the export cell lists: IDs, names, dates, teams, SEASON, the raw zone / distance / shot-type columns and the raw location, clock and action fields, which the engineered columns replace (same reasons as M.1). The engineered columns are Input. EVENT_TYPE (the target in disguise) is already removed from the export.
  3. Sample: give the three data sources the data roles Train, Validate and Test, so EM uses the same game-grouped 60/20/20 split as this notebook and its results are directly comparable. (A Data Partition node would split rows at random, so shots from one game would land in several partitions.)
  4. Explore: StatExplore, MultiPlot, Variable Selection, Cluster (on LOC_X, LOC_Y).
  5. Modify: Replacement (rare action levels, or use action_family), Transform Variables (log_dist is already provided), Impute.
  6. Model: Regression, Decision Tree, Neural Network, Gradient Boosting → Ensemble.
  7. Assess: Model Comparison with average squared error as the selection statistic. ASE is the Brier score, which ranks the models the same way as the log loss used here (A.1). Then Score nba_shots_2024_25_for_sas_scoring.csv (the 2024-25 season, also exported).
  8. Report: screenshot the diagram and the Model Comparison results; compare them with section A.1 in your article.
